tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

tools.name: pods_delete
tools.description: Delete a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

name.description: Name of the Pod to delete

namespace.description: Namespace to delete the Pod from

tools.name: pods_exec
tools.description: Execute a command in a Kubernetes Pod (shell access, run commands in container) in the current or provided namespace with the provided name and command

command.description: Command to execute in the Pod container. The first item is the command to be run, and the rest are the arguments to that command. Example: ["ls", "-l", "/tmp"]

container.description: Name of the Pod container where the command will be executed (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod where the command will be executed

namespace.description: Namespace of the Pod where the command will be executed

tools.name: pods_get
tools.description: Get a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod from

tools.name: pods_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_list_in_namespace
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes pods in the specified namespace in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter pods by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'spec.nodeName=node1'). Supported fields: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. Note: CrashLoopBackOff is a container state, not a pod phase, so it cannot be filtered directly. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label

tools.name: pods_log
tools.description: Get the logs of a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided name

container.description: Name of the Pod container to get the logs from (Optional)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the logs from

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pod logs from

tail.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, default: 100)

tools.name: pods_run
tools.description: Run a Kubernetes Pod in the current or provided namespace with the provided container image and optional name

image.description: Container Image to run in the Pod

name.description: Name of the Pod (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to run the Pod in

port.description: TCP/IP port to expose from the Pod container (Optional, no port exposed if not provided)

tools.name: pods_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Pods in the all namespaces, the provided namespace, or the current namespace

all_namespaces.description: If true, list the resource consumption for all Pods in all namespaces. If false, list the resource consumption for Pods in the provided namespace or the current namespace

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the pods by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Pod to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Pods in the namespace if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to get the Pods resource consumption from (Optional, current namespace if not provided and all_namespaces is false)

tools.name: projects_list
tools.description: List all the OpenShift projects in the current cluster

tools.name: resources_create_or_update
tools.description:
Create or update a Kubernetes resource via Server-Side Apply. The manifest is the complete desired state: any field this tool previously set and the new manifest omits is removed. To edit an existing resource, fetch it with resources_get, modify it, then re-apply the full resource.
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

resource.description: Complete YAML or JSON representation of the Kubernetes resource (full desired state, not a partial patch). Include apiVersion, kind, metadata, and the full spec.

tools.name: resources_delete
tools.description:
Delete a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, optionally the namespace, and its name
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

gracePeriodSeconds.description: Optional duration in seconds before the object should be deleted. Value must be non-negative integer. The value zero indicates delete immediately. If this value is nil, the default grace period for the specified type will be used

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to delete the namespaced resource from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will delete resource from configured namespace

tools.name: resources_get
tools.description:
Get a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, optionally the namespace, and its name
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the namespaced resource from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will get resource from configured namespace

tools.name: resources_list
tools.description:
List Kubernetes resources and objects in the current cluster by providing their apiVersion and kind and optionally the namespace and label selector
(common apiVersion and kind include: v1 Pod, v1 Service, v1 Node, apps/v1 Deployment, networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, route.openshift.io/v1 Route)

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resources (examples of valid apiVersion are: v1, apps/v1, networking.k8s.io/v1)

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter resources by field values (e.g. 'status.phase=Running', 'metadata.name=myresource'). Supported fields vary by resource type. For Pods: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, spec.restartPolicy, spec.schedulerName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.phase (Pending/Running/Succeeded/Failed/Unknown), status.podIP, status.nominatedNodeName. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

kind.description: kind of the resources (examples of valid kind are: Pod, Service, Deployment, Ingress)

labelSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'app=myapp,env=prod' or 'app in (myapp,yourapp)'), use this option when you want to filter the resources by label

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the namespaced resources from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will list resources from all namespaces

tools.name: resources_scale
tools.description: Get or update the scale of a Kubernetes resource in the current cluster by providing its apiVersion, kind, name, and optionally the namespace. If the scale is set in the tool call, the scale will be updated to that value. Always returns the current scale of the resource

apiVersion.description: apiVersion of the resource (examples of valid apiVersion are apps/v1)

kind.description: kind of the resource (examples of valid kind are: StatefulSet, Deployment)

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to get/update the namespaced resource scale from (ignored in case of cluster scoped resources). If not provided, will get/update resource scale from configured namespace

scale.description: Optional scale to update the resources scale to. If not provided, will return the current scale of the resource, and not update it

Done. Here’s what I set up:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matches stable)
  - Security config: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080)

Current state/validation
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 running (v2.0)
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 running (v2.1)
- Endpoints for Service now include 4 pods (2 from each deployment) on port 8080, which will split traffic roughly 50/50 by round-robin.

Notes and next steps
- Because both deployments have the same number of pods, traffic will be approximately 50/50. If one side scales differently (e.g., by HPA), the split will change proportionally.
- To skew traffic without a service mesh, adjust replicas (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- Rollback options:
  - Easiest: revert the Service selector to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
  - Or scale canary to 0 replicas.
- Promote canary: scale down or remove engine-v2-0 or update it to the canary image and restore the version selector if desired.

If you’d like, I can pin the Service back to version selectors and create a second Service plus a headless Service to manage more explicit weights, or integrate with a service mesh/ingress for precise traffic shaping.

Done. Here’s what I set up:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Replicas: 2
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
  - Container port: 80 (matches stable)
  - Security config: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine (removed version filter) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - Port config unchanged (port 80 -> targetPort 8080)

Current state/validation
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 running (v2.0)
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 running (v2.1)
- Endpoints for Service now include 4 pods (2 from each deployment) on port 8080, which will split traffic roughly 50/50 by round-robin.

Notes and next steps
- Because both deployments have the same number of pods, traffic will be approximately 50/50. If one side scales differently (e.g., by HPA), the split will change proportionally.
- To skew traffic without a service mesh, adjust replicas (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- Rollback options:

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What I found:
- The Deployment’s container was starting with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, which caused a CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed:
- Recreated the Deployment without the custom command/args so the nginx-unprivileged image uses its default entrypoint.
- Exposed containerPort 8080 (the nginx-unprivileged default).

Current status:
- Pod app-5c7bd5bd8f-zgw2t is Running (1/1), 0 restarts, in namespace crashloop-test.

Want me to add a Service to expose it, or set a readiness/liveness probe?

results.taskOutput:

- Root cause: The Deployment used an invalid image tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag), causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What I found
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns) was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Scheduler message: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC to use an available StorageClass:
  - Deleted Pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
  - Created a new PVC homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready (container nginx ready)

How to verify
- kubectl get pod -n homepage-ns homepage-pod
- kubectl get pvc -n homepage-ns homepage-pvc

Note
- If you intended to use a custom StorageClass named "sc", create that StorageClass or update your manifests to use an existing one (e.g., standard).

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What I found
- Pod homepage-pod (homepage-ns) was Pending because its PVC homepage-pvc referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Scheduler message: pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC to use an available StorageClass:
  - Deleted Pending PVC homepage-pvc (no data loss since it was never bound).
  - Created a new PVC homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready (container nginx ready)

How to verify
- kubectl get pod -n homepage-ns homepage-pod
- kubectl get pvc -n homepage-ns homepage-pvc

Note
- If you intended to use a custom StorageClass named "sc", create that StorageClass or update your manifests to use an existing one (e.g., standard).

results.taskOutput:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness/liveness probes were hitting http://:80 on /is_ready and /get_status (nonexistent paths on the default Nginx).
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- Result: probes failed (connection refused), the pod was never marked ready, and the Service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to use port 8080 and probe the root path:
  - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - livenessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left 80 present but unused; can remove if you want).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready
  - orders/webapp-7455c67864-w9t9s 1/1 Running, restarts: 0
- Service has ready endpoints:
  - webapp Endpoints -> 10.244.0.25:8080

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
- Optional: port-forward and open in a browser:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then visit http://localhost:8080

Do you want me to:
- remove the unused containerPort 80 for cleanliness, and/or
- create an Ingress/LoadBalancer to expose the app externally (if you have a domain/TLS requirements)?

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness/liveness probes were hitting http://:80 on /is_ready and /get_status (nonexistent paths on the default Nginx).
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- Result: probes failed (connection refused), the pod was never marked ready, and the Service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to use port 8080 and probe the root path:
  - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - livenessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left 80 present but unused; can remove if you want).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready
  - orders/webapp-7455c67864-w9t9s 1/1 Running, restarts: 0
- Service has ready endpoints:
  - webapp Endpoints -> 10.244.0.25:8080

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
- Optional: port-forward and open in a browser:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then visit http://localhost:8080

Do you want me to:
- remove the unused containerPort 80 for cleanliness, and/or
- create an Ingress/LoadBalancer to expose the app externally (if you have a domain/TLS requirements)?

outputSteps.content:
I investigated and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx-unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080, but:
  - Readiness/liveness probes were hitting http://:80 on /is_ready and /get_status (nonexistent paths on the default Nginx).
  - The Service targeted port 80.
- Result: probes failed (connection refused), the pod was never marked ready, and the Service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to use port 8080 and probe the root path:
  - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - livenessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 8080
  - Exposed containerPort 8080 (left 80 present but unused; can remove if you want).
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (Service port remains 80).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready
  - orders/webapp-7455c67864-w9t9s 1/1 Running, restarts: 0
- Service has ready endpoints:
  - webapp Endpoints -> 10.244.0.25:8080

How to verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy,po,svc
- Optional: port-forward and open in a browser:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - Then visit http://localhost:8080

Do you want me to:
- remove the unused containerPort 80 for cleanliness, and/or
- create an Ingress/LoadBalancer to expose the app externally (if you have a domain/TLS requirements)?

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permission on core/v1 pods, so listing pods was forbidden.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept: apps/deployments list
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds the Role to ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- As that service account, listing pods in simple-rbac-setup should now work:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expect: yes
  - Or use the SA’s kubeconfig/token to run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Optional (if you need more than list)
- Add verbs get, watch to the pods rule if you also want to get/watch pods.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permission on core/v1 pods, so listing pods was forbidden.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept: apps/deployments list
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds the Role to ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- As that service account, listing pods in simple-rbac-setup should now work:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expect: yes
  - Or use the SA’s kubeconfig/token to run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Optional (if you need more than list)
- Add verbs get, watch to the pods rule if you also want to get/watch pods.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role bound to your service account only allowed listing apps/deployments. It did not grant any permission on core/v1 pods, so listing pods was forbidden.

What I fixed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permission to list pods in the core API group.
  - Added: apiGroups: [""], resources: ["pods"], verbs: ["list"]
  - Kept: apps/deployments list
- Your existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already correctly binds the Role to ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- As that service account, listing pods in simple-rbac-setup should now work:
  - kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
  - Expect: yes
  - Or use the SA’s kubeconfig/token to run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

Optional (if you need more than list)
- Add verbs get, watch to the pods rule if you also want to get/watch pods.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service ClusterIP couldn’t reach any Pods.
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080 by default (non-root), but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: even if the selector matched, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail inside the Pod.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- Left type as ClusterIP and kept the same ClusterIP.

Post-fix verification
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx now show the Pod IP with port 8080.
- From an in-cluster test pod, HTTP requests to:
  - http://nginx:80 → 200
  - http://10.100.174.201:80 (the Service ClusterIP) → 200
- Cleaned up the temporary test pods after verification.

Current state
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster on port 80 (which forwards to container port 8080).
- If you were trying to access it from outside the cluster, note the Service is ClusterIP (internal only). You’ll need one of:
  - NodePort Service
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it)
  - Ingress (recommended) pointing to this Service on port 80/8080

Optional next steps (tell me if you want me to apply one)
- Expose externally via:
  - NodePort example: nodePort 30080 on port 80.
  - Ingress example: host like nginx.example.com routing to Service web/nginx port 80.
- Add containerPort: 8080 in the Deployment for clarity, and readiness/liveness probes on httpGet port 8080.

Would you like me to set up an Ingress or NodePort for external access? If so, provide the desired hostname or nodePort.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service ClusterIP couldn’t reach any Pods.
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080 by default (non-root), but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: even if the selector matched, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail inside the Pod.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- Left type as ClusterIP and kept the same ClusterIP.

Post-fix verification
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx now show the Pod IP with port 8080.
- From an in-cluster test pod, HTTP requests to:
  - http://nginx:80 → 200
  - http://10.100.174.201:80 (the Service ClusterIP) → 200
- Cleaned up the temporary test pods after verification.

Current state
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster on port 80 (which forwards to container port 8080).
- If you were trying to access it from outside the cluster, note the Service is ClusterIP (internal only). You’ll need one of:
  - NodePort Service
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it)
  - Ingress (recommended) pointing to this Service on port 80/8080

Optional next steps (tell me if you want me to apply one)
- Expose externally via:
  - NodePort example: nodePort 30080 on port 80.
  - Ingress example: host like nginx.example.com routing to Service web/nginx port 80.
- Add containerPort: 8080 in the Deployment for clarity, and readiness/liveness probes on httpGet port 8080.

Would you like me to set up an Ingress or NodePort for external access? If so, provide the desired hostname or nodePort.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label: app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no endpoints, so traffic to the Service ClusterIP couldn’t reach any Pods.
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080 by default (non-root), but the Service targeted port 80.
  - Result: even if the selector matched, traffic to targetPort 80 would fail inside the Pod.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080
- Left type as ClusterIP and kept the same ClusterIP.

Post-fix verification
- Endpoints for Service web/nginx now show the Pod IP with port 8080.
- From an in-cluster test pod, HTTP requests to:
  - http://nginx:80 → 200
  - http://10.100.174.201:80 (the Service ClusterIP) → 200
- Cleaned up the temporary test pods after verification.

Current state
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster on port 80 (which forwards to container port 8080).
- If you were trying to access it from outside the cluster, note the Service is ClusterIP (internal only). You’ll need one of:
  - NodePort Service
  - LoadBalancer Service (if your environment supports it)
  - Ingress (recommended) pointing to this Service on port 80/8080

Optional next steps (tell me if you want me to apply one)
- Expose externally via:
  - NodePort example: nodePort 30080 on port 80.
  - Ingress example: host like nginx.example.com routing to Service web/nginx port 80.
- Add containerPort: 8080 in the Deployment for clarity, and readiness/liveness probes on httpGet port 8080.

Would you like me to set up an Ingress or NodePort for external access? If so, provide the desired hostname or nodePort.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: Pods were unschedulable due to a nodeSelector on the Deployment: spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }. Your cluster has no nodes with that label, so both pods stayed Pending (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector).
- Because no pods were running, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 failed.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector constraint from the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment web-app-deployment: Available=True, ReadyReplicas=2/2.
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-h9774: Running (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-n2kql: Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now include pod IP 10.244.0.31:80 (and will include the second pod once ready), so traffic should route correctly.

Why the error occurred
- With no endpoints, the Service had nothing to send traffic to, resulting in connection refused from clients hitting the Service.

Recommended follow-ups
- If this app should target special nodes in some environments, use nodeSelector or node affinity only where those nodes exist (e.g., via separate overlays or environment-specific values).
- Consider adding health probes to the Deployment:
  - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80
  - livenessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80
- Quick test: from any pod in the cluster, curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local to confirm 200 OK.

Tell me if you want me to add the readiness/liveness probes or revert the node selector to a different label set.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Diagnosis
- Root cause: Pods were unschedulable due to a nodeSelector on the Deployment: spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }. Your cluster has no nodes with that label, so both pods stayed Pending (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector).
- Because no pods were running, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 failed.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector constraint from the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment web-app-deployment: Available=True, ReadyReplicas=2/2.
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-h9774: Running (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-n2kql: Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now include pod IP 10.244.0.31:80 (and will include the second pod once ready), so traffic should route correctly.

Why the error occurred
- With no endpoints, the Service had nothing to send traffic to, resulting in connection refused from clients hitting the Service.

Recommended follow-ups
- If this app should target special nodes in some environments, use nodeSelector or node affinity only where those nodes exist (e.g., via separate overlays or environment-specific values).
- Consider adding health probes to the Deployment:
  - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80
  - livenessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80
- Quick test: from any pod in the cluster, curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local to confirm 200 OK.

Tell me if you want me to add the readiness/liveness probes or revert the node selector to a different label set.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: Pods were unschedulable due to a nodeSelector on the Deployment: spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: { environment: production-gpu }. Your cluster has no nodes with that label, so both pods stayed Pending (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector).
- Because no pods were running, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so calls to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 failed.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector constraint from the Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment so it can schedule on available nodes.

Current state (verified)
- Deployment web-app-deployment: Available=True, ReadyReplicas=2/2.
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-h9774: Running (10.244.0.31)
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-n2kql: Running
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now include pod IP 10.244.0.31:80 (and will include the second pod once ready), so traffic should route correctly.

Why the error occurred
- With no endpoints, the Service had nothing to send traffic to, resulting in connection refused from clients hitting the Service.

Recommended follow-ups
- If this app should target special nodes in some environments, use nodeSelector or node affinity only where those nodes exist (e.g., via separate overlays or environment-specific values).
- Consider adding health probes to the Deployment:
  - readinessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80
  - livenessProbe: HTTP GET / on port 80
- Quick test: from any pod in the cluster, curl http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local to confirm 200 OK.

Tell me if you want me to add the readiness/liveness probes or revert the node selector to a different label set.

The multi-tenant dev environment has been created and secured as requested. Summary of what’s applied:

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled role=dev-namespace, env=dev)
- dev-shared (labeled role=dev-shared, env=dev)
- staging (labeled role=restricted, env=staging)
- prod (labeled role=restricted, env=prod)

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings in each dev-<name> namespace bind:
    - User: alice → dev-alice, bob → dev-bob, charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccount: respective -sa
    - To ClusterRole: admin (namespaced admin)
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to ClusterRole: view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster-admins inherently have access)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

NetworkPolicies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- In dev-* namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress + Egress)
  - Allow Egress to dev-shared namespace only
  - Allow Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services (kube-system, kube-public)
- In dev-shared:
  - Default deny + allow same-namespace traffic
  - Allow Ingress from all dev namespaces (role=dev-namespace)
  - Allow Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services
- In staging and prod:
  - Default deny + allow same-namespace only; Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services
- Result:
  - Cross-developer communication is blocked
  - Dev namespaces can reach only own namespace + dev-shared (+ DNS/system services)
  - Staging/prod fully isolated from dev namespaces

Notes and recommendations
- Authentication: We bound Users named “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie”. Ensure your auth provider issues these user identities (or adjust RoleBinding subjects to match your identities or groups).
- CNI requirement: NetworkPolicies require a policy-aware CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Kube-router).
- DNS scope (optional hardening): Currently, “system services” Egress allows traffic to kube-system/kube-public. For stricter least-privilege, we can replace that with an allow-egress policy restricted to DNS only (UDP/TCP 53) to coredns (k8s-app in [coredns, kube-dns]) and optionally specific ports/targets as needed. Tell me if you want me to apply that refinement.

Verification quick checks
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota
- kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebindings
- kubectl -n dev-bob get networkpolicy
- Try cross-namespace connectivity (should be blocked except dev-*>dev-shared)
- Confirm staging/prod contain only default-deny + same-namespace/system egress policies

If you’d like, I can generate a single consolidated YAML bundle or refine DNS egress to be port- and label-scoped.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

The multi-tenant dev environment has been created and secured as requested. Summary of what’s applied:

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled role=dev-namespace, env=dev)
- dev-shared (labeled role=dev-shared, env=dev)
- staging (labeled role=restricted, env=staging)
- prod (labeled role=restricted, env=prod)

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings in each dev-<name> namespace bind:
    - User: alice → dev-alice, bob → dev-bob, charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccount: respective -sa
    - To ClusterRole: admin (namespaced admin)
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to ClusterRole: view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster-admins inherently have access)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

NetworkPolicies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- In dev-* namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress + Egress)
  - Allow Egress to dev-shared namespace only
  - Allow Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services (kube-system, kube-public)
- In dev-shared:
  - Default deny + allow same-namespace traffic
  - Allow Ingress from all dev namespaces (role=dev-namespace)
  - Allow Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services
- In staging and prod:
  - Default deny + allow same-namespace only; Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services
- Result:
  - Cross-developer communication is blocked
  - Dev namespaces can reach only own namespace + dev-shared (+ DNS/system services)
  - Staging/prod fully isolated from dev namespaces

Notes and recommendations
- Authentication: We bound Users named “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie”. Ensure your auth provider issues these user identities (or adjust RoleBinding subjects to match your identities or groups).
- CNI requirement: NetworkPolicies require a policy-aware CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Kube-router).
- DNS scope (optional hardening): Currently, “system services” Egress allows traffic to kube-system/kube-public. For stricter least-privilege, we can replace that with an allow-egress policy restricted to DNS only (UDP/TCP 53) to coredns (k8s-app in [coredns, kube-dns]) and optionally specific ports/targets as needed. Tell me if you want me to apply that refinement.

Verification quick checks
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota
- kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebindings
- kubectl -n dev-bob get networkpolicy
- Try cross-namespace connectivity (should be blocked except dev-*>dev-shared)
- Confirm staging/prod contain only default-deny + same-namespace/system egress policies

If you’d like, I can generate a single consolidated YAML bundle or refine DNS egress to be port- and label-scoped.

outputSteps.content:
The multi-tenant dev environment has been created and secured as requested. Summary of what’s applied:

Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie (labeled role=dev-namespace, env=dev)
- dev-shared (labeled role=dev-shared, env=dev)
- staging (labeled role=restricted, env=staging)
- prod (labeled role=restricted, env=prod)

RBAC
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings in each dev-<name> namespace bind:
    - User: alice → dev-alice, bob → dev-bob, charlie → dev-charlie
    - ServiceAccount: respective -sa
    - To ClusterRole: admin (namespaced admin)
- Read-only to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binds Users (alice, bob, charlie) and SAs (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa) to ClusterRole: view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (only cluster-admins inherently have access)

ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

NetworkPolicies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all non-system namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- In dev-* namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (Ingress + Egress)
  - Allow Egress to dev-shared namespace only
  - Allow Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services (kube-system, kube-public)
- In dev-shared:
  - Default deny + allow same-namespace traffic
  - Allow Ingress from all dev namespaces (role=dev-namespace)
  - Allow Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services
- In staging and prod:
  - Default deny + allow same-namespace only; Egress to system namespaces for DNS/system services
- Result:
  - Cross-developer communication is blocked
  - Dev namespaces can reach only own namespace + dev-shared (+ DNS/system services)
  - Staging/prod fully isolated from dev namespaces

Notes and recommendations
- Authentication: We bound Users named “alice”, “bob”, and “charlie”. Ensure your auth provider issues these user identities (or adjust RoleBinding subjects to match your identities or groups).
- CNI requirement: NetworkPolicies require a policy-aware CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Kube-router).
- DNS scope (optional hardening): Currently, “system services” Egress allows traffic to kube-system/kube-public. For stricter least-privilege, we can replace that with an allow-egress policy restricted to DNS only (UDP/TCP 53) to coredns (k8s-app in [coredns, kube-dns]) and optionally specific ports/targets as needed. Tell me if you want me to apply that refinement.

Verification quick checks
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl -n dev-alice get resourcequota
- kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebindings
- kubectl -n dev-bob get networkpolicy
- Try cross-namespace connectivity (should be blocked except dev-*>dev-shared)
- Confirm staging/prod contain only default-deny + same-namespace/system egress policies

If you’d like, I can generate a single consolidated YAML bundle or refine DNS egress to be port- and label-scoped.
